N(0,1), with lambda_0 != lambda_1 in (0,1). The treatment omits this example. Its thm:p15-se-dependent (handbook/parts/p15/sequential-evidence.tex 141-151; annex 79-90) keeps almost-sure termination as a bare hypothesis and never establishes it for this or any other dependent process. (i) Wald's discretization route to arbitrarily fine approximations of gamma (p.136) and of EZ_n / E(n) (p.143) for nonlattice scores is not explained. thm:p15-se-finite-recursion (parts 297-317; annex 242-248) covers only finite alphabets, and the treatment says nothing about continuous scores, including its own normal case. (ii) The source's sample-size argument is missing from def:p15-se-normal-saving (360-386). sections.title: Stopping boundaries, error guarantees and expected sampling requirements

missing_pieces.duty: ED26-METHOD-sequential-evidence-C04 (partial): The handbook explains every approximation it uses itself: nominal boundaries (lines 153-173), neglected overshoot in ET and gamma-bar (lines 214-217 and 266-272), the normal saving (360-386), the transform and continuous density (411-475), and the finite and unbounded regimes (89-90, 99-118, 480-536). The success condition is still not plainly met across the selected source extent ('complete original ... stopping/error and sample-size arguments'). Inside ranges the handbook cites, the held Wald 1945 states two approximations it leaves unexplained. On p.136 (Section 3.4, cited at line 273), gamma can be approximated arbitrarily finely for a score law not on a lattice by replacing z with a discrete lattice law of small span. On p.143 (between (4.7) and (4.8), within (4.4)-(4.14) cited at line 218), the same holds for E Z_n and hence E(n). The handbook gives exact results only for lattice laws (lines 276-317) and prefix enumeration only for a finite nonlattice alphabet (lines 314-316). Annex lines 242-248 reject an 'unqualified grid approximation' without stating it. For continuous score laws, including the source's normal case, the handbook never says whether or when gamma and E(T) computed for the discretized law apply to the actual stopping procedure; the discretized law is a different procedure. Also unexplained from the cited ranges: gamma-bar minus gamma tends to zero as the score mean and variance tend to zero (p.135); (4.51) can be used when B>0 and the upper-exit probability is near one (p.151); and the nominal boundaries only increase E_i(n), so Table 1 understates the true saving (pp.133, 146, 148).

missing_pieces.duty: ED26-P15-CH-robust-sequential-endpoints-C012 (partial): Supply this exact entry's hypotheses. The entry thm:p15-singular-contamination-stopping (handbook/parts/p15/robust-sequential-endpoints.tex 318-348) never states its observation space and does not restrict the contaminating law H. Its exact claim sup_{R in H_1} E_R N_{a,b} = E_{Q_1} N_{a,b} = (1-(3/5)^r)/(2/5) and the annex argument (annex 486-514: 'its mass p at one ranges over [2/5,3/5]'; 'If no such observation has occurred by time r, the test exits at the lower boundary') hold only when the space is {0,1}. Under def:p15-sequential-endpoint-setting (arbitrary measurable space, H any probability) and the clipped-score convention of thm:p15-huber-contamination-pair (r=1 on the common null set, so l=4/5 there), take R=(4/5)P_1+(1/5)delta_x with x outside {0,1}. R lies in H_1, and at a=3c it gives P_R(N>3)=19/125>0. Hence E_R N >= 264/125 > 49/25 = E_{Q_1} N. The failure condition 'unstated assumption' holds. Owed: state X={0,1} (or restrict H to laws on {0,1}) as a hypothesis of the entry, or compute and prove the worst-case expected size over the full stated alternative class.
